seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
title: DSA: two pointers, sliding window, stack, binary search
description: Two pointers and sliding windows, monotonic stacks, and binary search including search on the answer, with the off-by-one and invariant traps interviewers probe.
source: LeetCode problem set and discuss; NeetCode roadmap; Cracking the Coding Interview; Oracle Java docs (ArrayDeque, Deque); Python docs (bisect), CPython bisect source

questions.prompt: Match each problem with the technique that solves it best.

right.text: Sliding window with a last-seen map
Sort, then fix one element and run two pointers

questions.explanation: Recognising the pattern from the statement is half the interview: "contiguous + constraint" suggests a window, "pairs in sorted data" suggests two pointers, "matching nested structure" a stack, "minimum value that is feasible" a binary search.

questions.prompt: This longest-substring-without-repeats loop sets left = last[c] + 1 whenever c was seen before (it forgets max(left, ...)). What does it return for "abba", whose correct answer is 2?
questions.explanation: On the second b, left moves to 2. On the final a, last[a] = 0 so left = 1: it moved BACK, the window "bba" has length 3. The fix is left = max(left, last[c] + 1), so left never decreases.

questions.prompt: Write a Java method int maxArea(int[] h) for "container with most water": the bars at indices l and r hold min(h[l], h[r]) * (r - l) water. Use two pointers starting at both ends.

checks.label: starts two pointers at the two ends and loops while l < r
computes the area with Math.min of the two heights
moves a pointer inward each step

questions.explanation: Always move the pointer at the shorter bar: the width only shrinks, so only a taller bar can improve the area. O(n) time, O(1) space.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: A sliding window loop with an inner while that moves the left pointer is still O(n) overall.
questions.reason: Each of the two pointers only moves forward and travels at most n positions in total.

whys.a: Correct: total pointer moves are at most 2n, so the nested loop is amortised linear.
whys.b: R is the actual reason, so "does not explain" is wrong.
whys.c: R is true, so c cannot be right.
whys.d: A is true, so d cannot be right.

questions.explanation: Count total pointer movement, not loop nesting. The same amortised argument makes the monotonic stack O(n).

questions.prompt: Complete the description of next greater element.
questions.text: Scan left to right keeping a monotonic {1} stack of {2}; while the new value is bigger than the one on top, {3} the stack and record the answer for it.
questions.explanation: Each index is pushed once and popped once, so the whole pass is O(n). Daily temperatures uses the same loop and stores i - popped index instead of the value.

questions.prompt: In modern Java code, java.util.Stack is the recommended class for a stack; ArrayDeque is only for queues.

options.why: ArrayDeque supports push, pop and peek as a stack and is also a queue, so the claim is false.
Right: Stack is a legacy synchronized Vector subclass, and the Deque Javadoc says to prefer Deque implementations for LIFO use.

questions.explanation: Use Deque<Integer> st = new ArrayDeque<>(); with push, pop and peek. ArrayDeque rejects null elements, which Stack allows.

questions.prompt: Write a Python function is_valid(s) that returns True when every bracket in s made of ()[]{} is closed by the right type in the right order.

checks.label: uses a list (or deque) as a stack
pops and compares on a closing bracket
maps bracket types to each other
returns whether the stack is empty at the end

questions.explanation: Two traps: popping from an empty stack on input like ")" and forgetting the final emptiness check on "((". An opening-map variant that pushes the expected closer also passes.

questions.prompt: What is the area of the largest rectangle in the histogram with bar heights [2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3]?
questions.explanation: Bars 5 and 6 form a rectangle of height 5 and width 2, area 10. Compare: bars 5,6,2,3 limited by height 2 give 8, and the whole histogram limited by height 1 gives 6. A monotonic increasing stack of indices finds the best rectangle in O(n).

questions.prompt: A loop uses while (lo <= hi) { int mid = (lo + hi) / 2; if (a[mid] < target) lo = mid; else hi = mid - 1; }. Which input shape makes it loop forever?

options.text: When a[mid] < target and mid == lo, e.g. lo = 0, hi = 1
options.why: Right: lo = mid never advances once mid == lo, so the interval stops shrinking; it must be lo = mid + 1.

options.text: When the array contains many repeated duplicate values
options.why: Duplicates only change which index is found, not termination.

options.text: When target is smaller than every element in the array
options.why: That path takes hi = mid - 1 each time and ends when hi < lo.

options.text: When the array length happens to be an odd number
options.why: Parity does not matter; the update lo = mid is the defect.

questions.explanation: Whenever you move a bound, move it past mid (mid + 1 or mid - 1) unless you deliberately use the half-open lo < hi template with hi = mid.

questions.prompt: Write a Java method int lowerBound(int[] a, int x) returning the first index i with a[i] >= x in a sorted array (a.length if none). Use a half-open range [lo, hi).

checks.label: uses a loop condition lo < hi
moves lo to mid + 1 when a[mid] < x

questions.explanation: One template covers "first position >= x", insertion point and first-true predicates. The closed [lo, hi] version with lo <= hi is equally valid if used consistently.

questions.prompt: In the worst case, how many midpoints are examined to find or rule out a value in a sorted array of 1,000,000 elements, with standard binary search making one probe per iteration?
questions.explanation: Each probe halves the range: 2^19 = 524,288 < 10^6 < 2^20 = 1,048,576, so floor(log2 n) + 1 = 20 probes.

questions.prompt: Koko must eat all piles within h hours at speed k bananas per hour (each hour she eats from one pile). Why can you binary search k?

options.text: Feasibility is monotonic in k: a faster speed never hurts.
options.why: Right: that monotonic yes/no predicate is the only requirement, so you search k in [1, max(piles)] for the first feasible value.

options.text: The piles array can be sorted first, which enables the search.
options.why: Sorting piles is irrelevant; the search runs on the speed range, not on the array.

options.text: The total number of bananas is always an exact power of two.
options.why: Nothing about the input needs to be a power of two.

options.text: The hours needed is a convex function of the eating speed.
options.why: Hours is non-increasing in speed, which is monotonic; convexity is not required for binary search.

questions.explanation: For piles [3,6,7,11] and h = 8 the answer is 4. The same pattern solves "capacity to ship packages within D days" and "split array largest sum": O(n log(max)) time.

questions.prompt: When searching a rotated sorted array without duplicates, such as [4,5,6,7,0,1,2], how do you decide which half is sorted at each step?

options.text: If a[lo] <= a[mid] the left half is sorted, else the right.
options.why: Right: the sorted half is the one that does not contain the rotation point; then test whether the target lies in its range.

options.text: Compare a[mid] with the target only, ignoring a[lo] and a[hi].
options.why: The target comparison alone cannot tell which side to discard because the array is not globally sorted.

options.text: Find the maximum first with a linear scan, then split there.
options.why: A linear scan makes it O(n); the whole point is O(log n).

options.text: Always search the left half first, then fall back to the right.
options.why: That is not a rule and loses the logarithmic bound.

questions.explanation: With duplicates (e.g. [1,1,1,0,1]) a[lo] == a[mid] == a[hi] cannot decide the sorted side, so the worst case degrades to O(n): a favourite follow-up.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Binary search on the answer for Koko runs in O(n log M), where M is the largest pile.
questions.reason: The piles array must be sorted before the search can run.

whys.a: A is true but R is false, so R cannot explain it.
whys.b: R is false: the piles can stay in any order; only the feasibility check is monotonic.
whys.c: Correct: the O(n log M) bound holds, but the search is over speeds 1..M and needs a monotonic feasible(k) predicate, not a sorted piles array.
whys.d: A is true (log M iterations, each an O(n) feasibility scan), so this is wrong.

questions.explanation: Each of log M iterations does an O(n) feasibility scan. The array need not be sorted: the requirement is that the predicate flips only once as k grows.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Python's bisect module are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: bisect_left(a, x) returns the index of the leftmost position where x could be inserted keeping order.
options.why: Right: for [1,2,2,2,3] and x = 2 it returns 1.

options.text: bisect_right(a, x) returns an insertion point after any existing entries equal to x.
options.why: Right: it returns 4 for the same list.

options.text: bisect works on an unsorted list as long as the values are comparable.
options.why: The list must already be sorted or the result is meaningless.

options.text: insort(a, x) inserts in O(log n) total time.
options.why: Finding the spot is O(log n) but shifting the list elements is O(n).

questions.explanation: Use bisect_left for lower bound and bisect_right for upper bound; `bisect_left(a, x)` equals count of elements < x.
